flashcards.q: Why does thread-per-connection I/O hit a wall around a few thousand connections (C10K)?
flashcards.a: Each thread needs its own stack (commonly 1-8MB reserved) and the kernel scheduler degrades juggling thousands of runnable/blocked threads; named by Dan Kegel's 1999 C10K essay.

flashcards.q: Why are select() and poll() O(n) per call?
flashcards.a: They are stateless across calls: the kernel re-scans the entire watched-fd list every call regardless of how many descriptors actually changed state.

flashcards.q: What is select()'s hard descriptor limit and why can't it just be raised?
flashcards.a: FD_SETSIZE, typically 1024 — a compile-time bitmap size baked into the ABI; raising it isn't portable and doesn't fix the underlying O(n)-per-call scan cost anyway.

flashcards.q: Why is epoll's epoll_wait O(1) per ready event instead of O(n)?
flashcards.a: The interest list lives in the kernel (a red-black tree via epoll_ctl) and driver callbacks push state changes onto a separate ready-list; epoll_wait only drains that ready-list.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between level-triggered and edge-triggered epoll?
flashcards.a: LT re-fires every call while the fd stays ready (forgiving). ET fires only on the ready-state transition, so a handler must read-loop until EAGAIN or it silently stalls.

flashcards.q: What does io_uring's SQ/CQ model avoid that epoll+read() doesn't?
flashcards.a: Submission entries are written into a shared-memory ring with no syscall; only io_uring_enter() is a syscall, and it can batch many operations at once instead of a syscall per operation.

flashcards.q: What does IORING_SETUP_SQPOLL do and what does it cost?
flashcards.a: A dedicated kernel thread polls the submission queue so steady-state submission needs zero syscalls — at the cost of that thread burning a full CPU core continuously.

flashcards.q: Is io_uring always faster than epoll?
flashcards.a: No — unbatched, one-operation-at-a-time io_uring can be slower than epoll because its setup/bookkeeping overhead isn't amortized; the win requires batching.

flashcards.q: Why has Google disabled io_uring by default in ChromeOS, Android, and production servers?
flashcards.a: Roughly 60% of Google's kCTF kernel bug-bounty submissions have targeted io_uring (~$1M paid), including CVE-2024-0582, a use-after-free giving read/write access to freed kernel pages.

flashcards.q: What does sendfile() save versus read()+write(), concretely?
flashcards.a: A measured 2.5GiB transfer took 2,972 syscalls with sendfile() versus 131,093 syscalls with read+write — about 44x fewer syscalls and zero userspace copies.

flashcards.q: When does zero-copy (sendfile/splice) provide no benefit?
flashcards.a: When the data must be transformed in userspace, e.g. on-the-fly gzip compression or encryption — the bytes must pass through userspace to be transformed, so the kernel-only copy path doesn't apply.

flashcards.q: When is mmap the wrong choice for reading a large file?
flashcards.a: For a one-pass sequential scan — mmap loses kernel readahead and pays a minor-fault cost (~1-10us) per first-touched page, often losing to a plain buffered read(); mmap wins for repeated random-access workloads.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between sendfile() and splice()?
flashcards.a: sendfile() is specifically file-to-socket (or similar); splice() is the general primitive moving data between a pipe and any other fd, which is how socket-to-socket proxying (nginx, HAProxy) stays zero-copy.
